traveler: Saint Anthony of Padua (Fernando of Lisbon, Antonius Patavinus)
title: The Kitchen at Montepaolo: Fernando of Lisbon, the Failed Martyrdom, and the Voice Padua Kept
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Lisbon, a son born without a date
stops.date_confidence: Year conventional, day not documented. The primitive thirteenth-century lives give neither birthdate nor parents' names; the exact date 15 August 1195 is flagged by the Basilica of Saint Anthony's own literature as a very late tradition, and the surname Martins de Bulhoes with the parents Vicente Martins and Teresa Pais Taveira comes from fifteenth-century writers, which Niccolo Dal-Gal (1907) judged less certain. Date entered as the traditional one so the segment orders; treat both day and surname as [R].
stops.campa: A son is born to a household of the parish beside the Lisbon cathedral, in a city a generation out of Moorish hands, and is called Fernando. The lives written within a year of his death give neither the day nor the names of his parents. The famous date, the fifteenth of August 1195, and the surname Martins de Bulhoes arrive two centuries later, and the basilica that keeps his bones marks the date in its own literature as a very late tradition. What the earliest text says is that he was born in Lisbon, of parents of some standing. About the birth it says nothing further.
suggested_refs: The traditional birthplace site beside the Se of Lisbon, later the church of Santo Antonio
sources: Basilica del Santo (santantonio.org), tradition notice on the birthdate
Assidua (Vita prima, c.1232), silent on birthdate and surname
Niccolo Dal-Gal (1907), via Wikipedia, 'Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Sao Vicente de Fora, the Augustinian habit at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Assidua; year conventional, month and day unknown and defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At about fifteen he takes the habit of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine at Sao Vicente de Fora, outside the walls, on the ground where Afonso Henriques buried the crusaders who took the city for him. He will spend eleven years in this order, longer than in the one that makes him famous, and nothing in the record suggests he entered it intending to leave. The canons keep choir, library, and school. The boy is set to the psalter, to Latin, and to the offices that cut the day into eight fixed pieces, the first of them sung in the dark before dawn.
suggested_refs: The Monastery of Sao Vicente de Fora, Lisbon, house of the Augustinian canons regular
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'St. Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Santa Cruz of Coimbra, eight years inside the books
stops.date_confidence: Transfer attested in the Assidua; the stated motive, that visiting Lisbon relatives broke his concentration, is later biographical gloss [R]. Year conventional, month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: Two years in, he asks to be moved inland to Santa Cruz at Coimbra, then the royal capital and the most serious school of scripture in Portugal. Later biographers explain the move by the traffic of Lisbon relatives coming to the parlour; the transfer is in the early sources, the motive is a gloss laid over it. At Coimbra he reads the Vulgate until it is furniture in his head, with the fathers and the allegorical machinery of the schools stacked around it. No one outside the cloister hears of him in these years. The reading goes on for roughly eight of them.
suggested_refs: The Monastery of Santa Cruz, Coimbra, and its twelfth-century scriptorium
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'St. Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Santa Cruz of Coimbra, the priesthood without a year
stops.date_confidence: [R]. No primitive source gives an ordination year and the Catholic Encyclopedia gives none. Wikipedia's 'ordained around age nineteen' would put it near 1214, which is incompatible with the 1219 sometimes printed in devotional chronologies. The defensible statement is 'a priest by 1220'; 1219 is entered only to order the segment, and the venue is inference from his residence.
stops.campa: He is ordained priest somewhere in these Coimbra years. No primitive source gives the year, the Catholic Encyclopedia gives none either, and the tradition that he was ordained at about nineteen would place it near 1214, which does not sit with the 1219 printed elsewhere. What can be said without straining is that he is a priest by 1220. One account adds that he was made guestmaster of the abbey, which would put him at the door of the house, receiving whoever came up the road from the south. Where the ordination happened, and at whose hands, no source says.
suggested_refs: The guest quarters of Santa Cruz, Coimbra, on the pilgrim road
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), which gives no ordination year
Centro Studi Antoniani, on the imprecision of the early chronology

stops.name: Santa Cruz of Coimbra, five bodies come back from Morocco
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Berard of Carbio and his four companions were beheaded in Morocco on 16 January 1220 and their major shrine is Santa Cruz, Coimbra. The date given is the martyrdom; the return of the relics follows within the year. The tradition crediting King Afonso II with ransoming the bodies is [R] and contested, a competing account crediting the Infante Dom Pedro, then in Morocco.
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of January five friars of a new and barely known order are beheaded at Marrakesh: Berard of Carbio and his companions, who had gone to preach to the Almohad caliph and refused every offer to stop. Fernando is a canon of a wealthy, settled, learned house with eight years of scripture behind him, and this is a mission his own order would never have sent anyone on. The bodies are ransomed and carried back over the strait to Coimbra. They are laid in Santa Cruz itself, in the church where he keeps choir.
suggested_refs: The shrine of Berard of Carbio and companions, Monastery of Santa Cruz, Coimbra

segments.name: The Name, and the Martyrdom That Would Not Come

stops.name: Santo Antonio dos Olivais, the change of habit and of name
stops.date_confidence: Year attested in the Assidua, month conventional. The location is contested: Wikipedia places the transfer at the hermitage of Olivais outside Coimbra, the Catholic Encyclopedia places it at Santa Cruz itself. The derivation of the new name from the hermitage's dedication to Anthony the Great is early but traditional [R].
stops.campa: Outside the city, at the small friars' house of Olivais, he asks for the habit of the Friars Minor and is given it. He puts down the name Fernando and takes the name of the hermitage's patron: Anthony, the Egyptian who walked into the desert nine hundred years before and whose life Athanasius wrote. Two saints will carry the one name into villages that keep both feasts and do not always keep them apart. He asks the friars for a single thing in exchange for what he is giving up, that they send him to Morocco.
suggested_refs: The hermitage church of Santo Antonio dos Olivais, above Coimbra, dedicated to Anthony the Great
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), which sites the change of habit at Santa Cruz instead

stops.name: Coimbra, the ship taken for Africa
stops.date_confidence: Departure attested in the Assidua; the month is conventional, the earliest sources not fixing the sailing date. Given as 1220-21 in the geography record.
stops.campa: He goes down to the sea with permission to follow the five where they went. The Franciscan mission to Morocco is nine months old and has already produced its martyrs, and that is precisely the attraction. Nothing in his conduct at this point looks like a career in the schools of Italy. He is a Portuguese priest of twenty-five who has read everything and wants to be killed for it in Africa, and the order that has just received him is young enough to let him try. The ship goes out of the Mondego in the autumn.
suggested_refs: The Mondego estuary and the Coimbra Franciscan community of 1220

stops.name: Morocco, the winter of the illness
stops.date_confidence: Illness and abandoned mission attested in the Assidua [A]; the specific town is not fixed by the earliest sources and Marrakesh is later inference from the 1220 martyrdoms [R]. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He reaches Morocco in the winter and falls sick almost at once, badly enough that he cannot preach and cannot stay. The earliest life gives the illness and the abandoned mission flatly, with no miracle attached and no town named; Marrakesh is where the five had died and is the town that tradition supplies. He is carried back to a ship having converted nobody and having been martyred by nobody. He is in Africa for one winter, and the earliest life does not say where in it.
suggested_refs: The Almohad capital of Marrakesh, site of the 1220 Franciscan martyrdoms

stops.name: The Atlantic off the Moroccan coast, the ship driven from its course
stops.date_confidence: Storm diversion attested early in the Assidua [A], but the Assidua fixes no position. This pin is a notional Atlantic point on the return route north of Larache, not a documented location; the older draft for this subject placed the landfall on the Sicilian coast between Tusa and Caronia instead. Month conventional.
stops.campa: The ship out of Morocco is bound for Portugal and does not reach it. Weather takes it off course somewhere in the Atlantic north of the Moroccan coast, and the earliest source records the diversion without a latitude. Whatever the master intended, the vessel ends up running east through the strait and along the whole length of the Mediterranean. A sick friar with no assignment left is carried past Spain, past Sardinia, and set down at the far end of Sicily.
suggested_refs: The Atlantic return route from Morocco to Portugal, and the storm season of early 1221
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'St. Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Messina, taken in by the friars
stops.date_confidence: Sicilian landfall and recovery attested in the Assidua; month conventional, fixed only by the need to reach Assisi by Pentecost.
stops.campa: The friars at Messina take him in and feed him back into health. He is nobody here: a foreign priest with a Portuguese accent, no province, no letters, and a failed mission behind him. What he has is the news that a general chapter is called at Assisi for Pentecost and that every brother who can walk is expected to be at it. So he walks the length of Italy, from the Sicilian shore to Umbria, on foot, in spring, in a habit he has worn for a year, and reaches Assisi by Pentecost.
suggested_refs: The early Franciscan house at Messina, first Italian shelter of the shipwrecked friar

segments.name: The Chapter of Mats and the Hermitage

stops.name: The Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats
stops.date_confidence: Chapter date attested: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives the general chapter at Assisi as 30 May 1221, and Pentecost fell on that day. Anthony's presence is attested. A personal encounter with Francis of Assisi at the chapter is [R] and drops out of the record: no early source describes a meeting, the Assidua has him left unassigned and then taken by Brother Gratian into Romagna, and Wikipedia says only that he later came to Francis's attention. Pin inherited byte-identical from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: Pentecost, and the plain below Assisi fills with brothers camped under mats and wattle, some five thousand of them, which is why the chapter keeps the name. Francis of Assisi presides with his voice already failing and has Elias speak for him. The long Rule is read out to the whole encampment. Anthony stands somewhere in that crowd with no province willing to claim him, and when the provincials disperse he is left over, unassigned, until Brother Gratian of Romagna takes him. No early text records the two men speaking to each other.
suggested_refs: The Porziuncola chapel at Santa Maria degli Angeli and the encampment of the 1221 chapter
saint_francis.journey.json, stop 'Porziuncola, the Chapter of Mats', which names the unknown Portuguese in the crowd
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'General Chapter: Assisi, 30 May 1221'

stops.name: Montepaolo, the hermitage above Dovadola
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Assidua; sources disagree on duration, one giving c.1221-1222 and another 1222-1227. The Italian record for the Eremo di Montepaolo dates the stay 1221-1222 with a later return c.1228 as provincial, which resolves part of the spread. Month conventional.
stops.campa: Gratian sends him seven kilometres out of Dovadola to the hermitage of Montepaolo, where a handful of brothers keep a cell in the rock and say the hours. He asks for the kitchen and the dishes. He tells nobody that he has eight years of Coimbra behind him, or that he was a canon regular with a library before he was a friar with a bowl. The best-trained man in the province of Romagna washes pots on a hillside above the Montone valley. The sources give the stay as 1221 to 1222, about a year.
stops.quote: The saints are like the stars. In his providence Christ conceals them in a hidden place that they may not shine before others when they might wish to do so.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Anthony of Padua at catholicsaints.info, which names no work, sermon, or edition; not traced to the Sermones or any critical text
suggested_refs: The Eremo di Montepaolo above Dovadola, and the cave cell shown as his

stops.name: Forli, the sermon nobody had prepared
stops.date_confidence: Sharp source disagreement, not resolved: Wikipedia gives 1222, the Catholic Encyclopedia 1224, Franciscan Media c.1227. Month and day unknown, defaulted. The discovery narrative is hagiographically shaped in form [R]; his emergence as a major preacher in the early 1220s is well grounded [A].
stops.campa: An ordination brings Dominicans and Franciscans together at Forli, and afterward it turns out that nobody has prepared a word. The superior orders the Portuguese to say whatever the Holy Spirit gives him, on the safe assumption that he will say very little. He preaches, and the room understands within minutes that it has been keeping a scholar in a kitchen. The earliest life tells it in exactly this shape, which is the shape such stories always take, and the sources cannot agree whether the year was 1222, 1224, or 1227.
stops.quote: We should speak, then, as the Holy Spirit gives us the gift of speech.
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, sermon, second reading of the Office of Readings for 13 June, quoted at catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The Franciscan house at Forli and the 1222 ordination gathering

stops.name: Bologna, Santa Maria delle Pugliole: the brothers taught theology
stops.date_confidence: The letter of Francis of Assisi to Brother Anthony is a primary source generally accepted as authentic [A]; Wikipedia dates the entrustment to 1224, month and day unknown. The venue is corrected here: the Basilica of San Francesco in Bologna was not begun until 1236, five years after Anthony's death, so the teaching cannot have happened there. The friars in Bologna were at the Santa Maria delle Pugliole house from 1211.
stops.campa: Sent to the friars' house at Santa Maria delle Pugliole, he begins to teach theology to brothers who have until now been told that books are a danger to them. Francis settles the question in a letter of four lines: he is content that Anthony teach the brothers sacred theology, provided the study does not put out the spirit of prayer and devotion. It is the earliest permission of its kind in the order, and the Franciscans date their school tradition from it. The permission and the condition on it stand in the same sentence.
stops.quote: I would like you to teach the brethren theology
stops.quote_source: Francis of Assisi, letter to Brother Anthony, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The letter of Francis of Assisi to Brother Anthony, the order's founding charter of study
sources: Letter of Francis of Assisi to Brother Anthony (primary source, generally accepted)

stops.name: Bologna, the psalter taken and brought back
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The story is absent from the Assidua and appears only in much later Franciscan tradition; the date is a placeholder inside the Bologna years and carries no independent authority.
stops.campa: A novice leaves the order and takes with him Anthony's psalter, a working copy annotated in his own hand for teaching, which is to a lecturing friar what a set of tools is to a carpenter. The story says he prayed and the man came back with the book. None of this is in the life written within a year of his death; it surfaces much later. On that one anecdote rests his standing as the patron of lost things, of keys, wallets, wedding rings, and missing persons. The Assidua does not mention a psalter at all, stolen or otherwise.
suggested_refs: The lost-psalter legend and its later devotional literature

segments.name: North of the Sea: The French Years

stops.name: Montpellier, the lector sent into Languedoc
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Catholic Encyclopedia's chronology sends him from Bologna through Montpellier and Toulouse; the wider southern itinerary is broadly accepted in outline but not independently confirmed by the Assidua, and many local episodes rest on Jean Rigaud's Rigaldina of c.1300. Month conventional.
stops.campa: He is sent north of the sea into Languedoc, where the order wants preachers who can argue and where the Albigensian war has been running for fifteen years. At Montpellier he lectures. What survives from his own hand is the sermons, and the sermons are addressed to preachers rather than to crowds. The itinerary through southern France is accepted in outline by everyone and fixed in detail by almost nothing: most of the local episodes come from Jean Rigaud's life, written around 1300, seventy years downstream of the man it describes.
suggested_refs: Jean Rigaud, Rigaldina (c.1300), principal source for the French episodes
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'St. Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Toulouse, preaching in the Cathar country
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Presence broadly accepted, dating soft, month and day unknown and defaulted. No reliable text preserves anything he said in the city; the quote below is from the sermon corpus, not from a Toulouse occasion.
stops.campa: He preaches at Toulouse, in a country where a Cathar church had kept its own bishops and its own liturgy and where the Dominicans had been founded to argue with it. What survives of his method is in the model sermons, and there he goes at pride, wealth, and hardness far more often than at doctrine: the mark of the Spirit, in his account, is not an argument won but a way of living that other people can see. No reliable text records a single sentence he spoke in the city.
stops.quote: The man who is filled with the Holy Spirit speaks in different languages. These different languages are different ways of witnessing to Christ, such as humility, poverty, patience and obedience; we speak in those languages when we reveal in ourselves these virtues to others.
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, Sermones I, 226, second reading of the Office of Readings for 13 June (Liturgy of the Hours), via the archived liturgies.net page
suggested_refs: The Franciscan and Dominican convents of Toulouse in the years after the Albigensian war
sources: web.archive.org snapshot of liturgies.net, 'St Anthony of Padua, readings'

stops.name: Arles, the chapter and the vision in the doorway
stops.date_confidence: Chapter attendance [R], widely accepted but from Wikipedia's chronology rather than a primary source, and contradicted by the Catholic Encyclopedia, which puts him in the Limousin in this year. The bilocation story, in which Francis appears beside him though absent in body, is a much later hagiographic accretion, separate from the chapter itself. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: He attends a Franciscan chapter at Arles and preaches to the assembled brothers on the title nailed over the cross. He is thirty-one, and by now the most sought-after preacher the order has north of the Alps. Later Franciscan tradition puts Francis of Assisi in the doorway of that chapter room, absent in body and visible to everyone in it, arms raised, blessing them. That story appears well after the earliest life and grew separately from the chapter attendance itself, which nobody disputes.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan chapter house at Arles and the later bilocation legend
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), which contradicts this itinerary

stops.name: Brive, custos of the Limousin
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The Catholic Encyclopedia makes him Custos Provincial of the Limousin in 1226, which flatly contradicts Wikipedia's Arles and Provence chronology for the same year. Both are recorded here; neither is adjudicated. Month conventional. The local episodes derive from the Rigaldina (c.1300).
stops.campa: He is given the custody of the Limousin, an administrative charge over the houses of the province, and preaches through the country around Brive. The Limousin remembers him in caves, grottoes, and roadside chapels, most of it written down first by Rigaud around 1300, and the grottoes are still shown. The Catholic Encyclopedia puts him here in the same year that other chronologies have him in Provence, and others again on the road back to northern Italy. The three itineraries cannot be reconciled and are not reconciled here.
suggested_refs: The grotto of Saint Anthony at Brive-la-Gaillarde and the Limousin traditions collected by Rigaud
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'Custos Provincial in the Limousin, 1226'

stops.name: Padua, the return and the office
stops.date_confidence: Francis of Assisi's death on 3 October 1226 is attested and is given by the Catholic Encyclopedia as the occasion of Anthony's return. The senior office is attested [A] but its name and year are not: Wikipedia gives provincial minister of northern Italy or Romagna by c.1227, the Catholic Encyclopedia makes him Minister Provincial of Emilia shortly after his return. Modern Franciscan historiography warns against projecting later territorial terminology onto the still-informal structure. Month defaulted.
stops.campa: Francis of Assisi dies at the Porziuncola on the third of October 1226, and Anthony crosses back into Italy. Within months he holds a senior charge over the friars of the north, called in the sources provincial minister of Romagna, or of Emilia, though the order's structure at this date is loose enough that the title is heavier than the thing it names. Padua becomes the place he comes back to rather than the place he governs from. He is on the road for most of the year: Venice, the Friuli, Istria, the Po towns.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan province of northern Italy in the years immediately after Francis's death
sources: Dialogus de gestis sanctorum fratrum Minorum (c.1245-46)

stops.name: Rimini, the shore and the fish
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Absent from the Assidua and attested only in later hagiographic layers; undated within his lifetime, so the year is a placeholder inside the northern provincial period. No monument fixes the site: the Tempietto di Sant'Antonio at Rimini commemorates the mule, not the fish, and should not be attached to this scene.
stops.campa: The story is that the town would not listen, so he went down to the water and preached to the fish, and the fish came up in ranks with their heads out of the water and held still until he had finished and blessed them, and the town came down to the shore to watch. It is not in the earliest life. It appears decades later, and it is the image of him that outran every other, painted, carved, and set into rhyme across Europe. No monument marks the place, and no source names the stretch of shore.
suggested_refs: The sermon to the fish in the later Franciscan legendaries and its European iconography
sources: Later Franciscan legendary tradition, well after the Assidua

stops.name: Rimini, the mule that would not eat
stops.date_confidence: [R]. Later Franciscan legend, not in the Assidua, undated; year and month are placeholders. Traditionally sited at Rimini, where the Tempietto di Sant'Antonio in Piazza Tre Martiri marks the spot, though other versions of the story place it elsewhere on his itinerary.
stops.campa: A man who denies the real presence in the sacrament proposes a test: starve his mule three days, then set fodder in front of the animal and the host beside the fodder, and let it choose. The mule is said to have walked past the barley and knelt. A small round chapel on the square where three partisans were shot seven centuries later marks the place for the version that fixes the story at Rimini; other versions put it at Toulouse or at Bourges. None of them is in the Assidua.
stops.quote: If you preach Jesus, he will melt hardened hearts; if you invoke him he will soften harsh temptations; if you think of him he will enlighten your mind; if you read of him he will satisfy your intellect
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, Sermones, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The Tempietto di Sant'Antonio, Piazza Tre Martiri, Rimini, built over the traditional site of the mule

stops.name: Rome, before Gregory IX and the court
stops.date_confidence: Papal audience in 1228 confirmed, month conventional. The epithet is transmitted in two forms and both are given: the English tradition has Ark of the Testament, Doctor arca testamenti; the Italian tradition has both arca del Testamento and scrigno, the jewel case or treasury of the Bible. The commission for festal sermons is attributed by the Italian source to Cardinal Rinaldo Conti, later Alexander IV, not directly to Gregory IX.
stops.campa: Called to the papal court, he preaches before Gregory IX and the cardinals and to an audience of clerics from every language in Latin Christendom. The pope's phrase for him afterwards goes into every later life: the Ark of the Testament, a man carrying the whole of scripture inside him and able to open it at will. Around this time a cardinal, Rinaldo Conti, asks him for a written cycle of sermons for the feasts, and he begins the only work of his that survives. The Italian tradition adds a second epithet for him: scrigno, the jewel case of the Bible.
stops.quote_source: Pope Gregory IX on Anthony after hearing him preach, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The papal court of Gregory IX at the Lateran, 1228
The commission of the Sermones in Festivitates, attributed to Cardinal Rinaldo Conti
sources: Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)

stops.name: The Porziuncola, the office laid down
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives the resignation of the office of Minister Provincial of Emilia at the general chapter of Assisi, 30 May 1230. The verified pool's chronology mislocated this resignation at Padua; the chapter was at Assisi, and Padua is where he then settled. Pin inherited byte-identical from saint_francis.journey.json.
stops.campa: At the general chapter at Assisi he gives up the province. He has held it three years, he is thirty-five, and what he asks for instead is time to preach, to hear confessions, and to write. The same chapter sends him to Rome in an embassy over the binding force of the Testament of Francis, a document already splitting the order between the brothers who want the Rule kept as written and the brothers who want it made livable. He goes to Rome with the embassy, and afterwards returns to Padua.
suggested_refs: The general chapter of Assisi, 30 May 1230, and the dispute over the Testament of Francis
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (New Advent), 'General Chapter of Assisi, 30 May 1230'

stops.name: Padua, the sermons written for other men's mouths
stops.date_confidence: Composition in the final Padua years, c.1229-31; month and day unknown and defaulted. The securely authentic corpus is principally the Sermones dominicales et festivi; the far longer lists of works under his name in early-modern bibliographies do not survive examination.
stops.campa: He writes the Sermones dominicales et festivi, a cycle of model sermons in dense scholastic Latin, built out of concordance, allegory, and the four senses, and meant for other preachers to take apart and use. They are not transcripts of anything said to a crowd. Modern scholarship counts them as very nearly the whole of what can safely be called his, and the long lists of works printed under his name in the early modern bibliographies do not survive examination.
stops.quote: Actions speak louder than words; let your words teach and your actions speak. We are full of words but empty of actions, and therefore are cursed by the Lord, since he himself cursed the fig tree when he found no fruit but only leaves.
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, sermon, second reading of the Office of Readings for 13 June (Liturgy of the Hours), cross-checked at catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: Sermones dominicales et festivi ad fidem codicum recogniti, 3 vols., Centro Studi Antoniani, Padua, 1979
sources: Modern Antonian scholarship on the authentic corpus

stops.name: Padua, the Lent of thirty thousand
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to the number. The Catholic Encyclopedia reports crowds exceeding thirty thousand for the final Lenten series; medieval crowd figures of this kind are conventional and not verifiable. The preaching itself, and its subjects, are attested in the Dialogus and reflected in his own sermon corpus. Month fixed by Lent, day unknown.
stops.campa: He preaches the whole of Lent in Padua and the city cannot hold the crowds. The Catholic Encyclopedia repeats a figure of thirty thousand; whatever the true count, the sermons go outdoors and the shops close. He preaches against usury and against the private wars of the Paduan families, and the two subjects are one subject, because the debt that ruins a household and the faction that burns it are run by the same men. He hears confessions from first light until he cannot stand.
stops.quote: O rich people, befriend... the poor, welcome them into your homes: it will subsequently be they who receive you in the eternal tabernacles in which is the beauty of peace, the confidence of security and the opulent tranquillity of eternal satiety
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, Sermones, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va); ellipsis as given in the quoted excerpt
suggested_refs: The open-air Lenten preaching of 1231 in Padua, and the confessional queues recorded with it
sources: Dialogus de gestis sanctorum fratrum Minorum (c.1245-46)

stops.name: Padua, the debt law changed at his asking
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and unusually well: the podesta Stefano Badoer amended the Paduan law of debt on 15 March 1231, and the civic act names Anthony in its own wording, ad preces venerabilis fratris beati Antonii. This is documentary, not devotional attribution, and is a firmer class of evidence than anything in the miracle collections.
stops.campa: On the fifteenth of March the podesta of Padua, Stefano Badoer, amends the city's law of debt. An insolvent man who surrenders his assets may no longer be imprisoned or driven into exile for what is still owed. The act says in its own text that it is made ad preces venerabilis fratris beati Antonii, at the entreaty of the venerable brother, blessed Anthony. He is named there, while he is alive, in the civic register of a north Italian commune. The clause stands in the statute book under that date.
stops.quote: Charity is the soul of faith, it gives it life; without love, faith dies
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, Sermones, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The Paduan debtors' statute of 15 March 1231 and the civic register of the podesta Stefano Badoer
sources: Municipal statute of Padua, 15 March 1231 (documented civic record)

stops.name: Verona, before Ezzelino da Romano
stops.date_confidence: Weakly held. The episode appears in later Franciscan lives and in the earlier draft file for this subject; no early chronology in the verified record carries it, and no other researched file corroborates it. Month conventional. Kept, flagged, and not adjudicated.
stops.campa: He goes to Verona to ask Ezzelino da Romano, who holds the March by terror and is keeping Paduan prisoners, for their release. Ezzelino does not release them. It is the last thing he is said to have attempted while he can still sit a horse: the preacher against faction, put in front of the man the factions had produced. He rides back toward Padua with nothing, and is dead within six weeks. The episode belongs to the later lives rather than to the earliest one, no primary chronology carries it, and it is kept here flagged rather than dropped.
suggested_refs: The court of Ezzelino III da Romano at Verona, 1231
sources: st_anthony_of_padua.journey.json (earlier draft file in this checkout)

stops.name: Camposampiero, the cell built in the walnut tree
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Assidua and among the earliest-attested episodes of the death sequence. The Italian record for the Santuario del Noce dates the stay c.19 May to 13 June 1231 and names Count Tiso VI as the builder of the structure in the tree. The attribution of the illness to ergotism is [R], from one source only.
stops.campa: Count Tiso VI has a platform built for him in the branches of a walnut tree at Camposampiero, north of Padua, and he lives in it for something under a month: a friar of thirty-five up a tree, coming down for the office and for food he cannot keep. From the branches he can see the road south to the city he has decided to be buried in. His legs have swollen and his breath is short. One tradition names ergotism, the fire in the rye that ran through the Veneto in that century, and it is a single source that names it.
stops.quote: Christ who is your life is hanging before you, so that you may look at the Cross as in a mirror. There you will be able to know how mortal were your wounds, that no medicine other than the Blood of the Son of God could heal.
stops.quote_source: Anthony of Padua, Sermones, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The Santuario del Noce, Camposampiero, built over the site of the walnut-tree cell

stops.name: Arcella, the cart stops short of the city
stops.date_confidence: Death date and place agreed across all sources: 13 June 1231, at Arcella, in the Poor Clares' hospice, in a cell later enclosed by the sanctuary church. The age is unstable: English and Italian Wikipedia both give 35, the Arcella sanctuary page gives 36. The death-scene details are early, from the Assidua dossier, and still [R] as legendary furniture rather than verified fact.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of June they load him on a cart to carry him into Padua and he does not get there. At Arcella, just outside the walls, at the house of the Poor Clares, he asks to be set down, is anointed, and dies. He is thirty-five, thirty-six by the reckoning the sanctuary itself prefers. The earliest account has him singing a Marian hymn, saying that he sees the Lord, and the children of Padua crying in the streets that the saint is dead before anyone had told them. Those details are the account's furniture, and the account is as early as anything there is.
suggested_refs: The Santuario dell'Arcella, Padua, enclosing the cell in which he died

stops.name: Padua, Santa Maria Mater Domini: the burial
stops.date_confidence: Burial at the Franciscan church of Santa Maria Mater Domini is attested; the four-day interval and the dispute over the body come from the Franciscan tradition rather than from a dated civic act, so the day is [R]. The church survives absorbed into the basilica as the Cappella della Madonna Mora.
stops.campa: Four days of argument over the body: Arcella wants it, the friars want it, the commune settles it, and on the seventeenth he is buried at Santa Maria Mater Domini, the small Franciscan church inside Padua that he had chosen for himself. Under everything the next six centuries would pile on top of the place, the grave is a hole in the floor of a small church. That church is still standing, swallowed whole by what grew around it, kept now as the chapel of the Madonna Mora, the Dark Madonna.
suggested_refs: The Cappella della Madonna Mora, the surviving fabric of Santa Maria Mater Domini inside the basilica
sources: Dialogus de gestis sanctorum fratrum Minorum (c.1245-46)

stops.name: Spoleto, canonized in under a year
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the papal act: Gregory IX canonized him at Spoleto on 30 May 1232, three hundred and fifty-two days after his death. The dossier drew on collected and investigated miracle reports, fifty-one by the basilica's count; that such reports were gathered and used procedurally is demonstrable by historical method, which does not itself adjudicate the causation claimed in them.
stops.campa: Three hundred and fifty-two days after his death Gregory IX canonizes him at Spoleto, the miracle reports having been gathered and examined, fifty-one of them by the basilica's count. A canonization inside a year, for a Portuguese friar who had been in Italy nine years and held no office when he died. Whether the reports describe what they claim to describe is not a question a chronology can settle; that they were gathered and acted on inside twelve months is documented. The Assidua is written in the same months, on the threshold of the act.
suggested_refs: The canonization bull of Gregory IX, Spoleto, 30 May 1232
The Assidua, written on the threshold of the canonization
sources: Papal act of canonization, Gregory IX, 30 May 1232

stops.name: Padua, the basilica goes up around the grave
stops.date_confidence: Construction begun c.1232 and largely complete by 1310, per the basilica's own institutional history and the English Wikipedia infobox; structural work continued into the mid-fifteenth century. The verified pool carried both 1301 and 1301-1310, standardized here to 1310. Month conventional.
stops.campa: Construction starts almost at once on a church large enough for the traffic. It goes up around the old one and absorbs it, and is largely finished by 1310: domes, a Byzantine roofline, and a scale altogether out of proportion to a man who asked to be buried in a friars' chapel. Padua calls the building il Santo and calls him il Santo, so that inside the city he has no name, only the article. Two of its chapels keep fourteenth-century fresco cycles, entered on the world heritage list in 2021.
suggested_refs: Donatello's bronze high altar for the Santo, c.1446-1450, with the Madonna and Child flanked by Francis, Anthony, Justina, Daniel, Louis, and Prosdocimus
Titian's three frescoes of Anthony's posthumous miracles, Scuola del Santo, April to December 1511
The nine marble reliefs of the Cappella dell'Arca, 1505-1577, by Antonio and Tullio Lombardo, Antonio Minello, Giovanni Maria Mosca, Sansovino, Danese Cattaneo and Girolamo Campagna
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Basilica of Saint Anthony of Padua'

stops.name: Padua, the tomb opened and the tongue found
stops.date_confidence: The first translation of the body is attested by an inscription of 1263 in the basilica's reliquary chapel. Month and day unknown and defaulted. Bonaventure's presence at the opening is given by the Catholic Encyclopedia; the report of the tongue found incorrupt while the rest had gone to bone is the tradition's own account of what was seen, recorded at the time and not independently testable now.
stops.campa: The relics are carried into the new church and the tomb is opened, an inscription in the reliquary chapel dating this first translation to 1263. The body has gone to bone and dust. The tongue is reported found whole and red, and Bonaventure, minister general and present at the opening, is said to have taken it in his hands and spoken to it. It is kept, and is kept still, in a silver-gilt reliquary eighty-one centimetres high; the jaw goes into a bust reliquary commissioned in 1349, and both stand in the treasury chapel begun in 1691.
suggested_refs: The reliquary of the tongue by Giuliano da Firenze and the 1349 chin reliquary, Treasury Chapel of the Basilica del Santo
sources: Basilica inscription of 1263, via it.wikipedia.org, 'Basilica di Sant'Antonio da Padova'

stops.name: Vatican City, the title Doctor Evangelicus
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives 16 January 1946. Explicitly a twentieth-century retrospective honour, not a contemporary thirteenth-century designation, and the campa says so.
stops.campa: Pius XII declares him a Doctor of the Church and gives him a title nobody in the thirteenth century would have recognized: Doctor Evangelicus, the evangelical doctor. It rests on the sermons, read seriously for the first time in centuries, and not on the fish, the mule, the psalter, or the tongue. Seven hundred and fifteen years after the funeral the church names him for the one thing he left in writing. The critical edition of those sermons will not be published until 1979.
stops.quote_source: Title conferred by Pope Pius XII proclaiming Anthony a Doctor of the Church, 1946, quoted in Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)
suggested_refs: The declaration of Anthony as Doctor of the Church, 16 January 1946
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia update / Wikipedia, 'Anthony of Padua'
Pope Benedict XVI, General Audience, 10 February 2010 (vatican.va)

stops.name: Padua, the tomb opened again with instruments
stops.date_confidence: Attested: John Paul II authorized the examination on 1 January 1981 and the tomb was opened five days later. The finding reported was that the vocal apparatus had remained intact; the connection drawn between that and his fame as a preacher is a devotional reading of an anatomical report, not a finding of it. The 1979 critical edition and Amandine Postec's BnF NAL 3245 identification are separately sourced.
stops.campa: John Paul II authorizes an examination of the remains on the first of January and the tomb is opened five days later, with anatomists present. The skeleton is measured and described. The report notes the vocal apparatus intact, which the devotion reads straight back into the preaching, and a new reliquary is made for it that year by Carlo Balljana. Two years earlier the Centro Studi Antoniani had published the three-volume critical edition of the sermons; afterward Amandine Postec finds fragments in a Paris manuscript that the edition's stemma does not account for.
suggested_refs: The 1981 reliquary by Carlo Balljana
Amandine Postec on the Anthony fragments in BnF NAL 3245, a textual branch absent from the 1979 stemma
sources: Centro Studi Antoniani, Sermones dominicales et festivi ad fidem codicum recogniti (1979)
